task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: What are rare earth elements and why are they considered critical to technology and national security? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of June 18, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Rare earth elements are a group of 17 metallic elements, including the 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium; despite their name, most are more abundant in Earth's crust than gold or platinum.
They are called 'rare' not because they are scarce globally but because they rarely occur in concentrated, economically mineable deposits; they are typically dispersed through rock in small amounts.

Neodymium and dysprosium are used in the strongest permanent magnets known — neodymium-iron-boron magnets — which are essential for electric vehicle motors, wind turbine generators, and military precision guidance systems.
Europium and terbium are used in phosphors that produce the colors in LED displays and fluorescent lighting.
Lanthanum is used in catalytic converters for gasoline vehicles and in specialized optical glass.

China mines approximately 60% of global rare earth supply and processes approximately 85% of the world's rare earth oxides; this concentration of refining capacity creates significant supply chain risk for other countries.

Materials scientist Dr. Anika Patel of Ridgeline Institute of Technology said: "The mining part is solvable. The refining part is where most countries have fallen behind — it took China decades to build that capacity, and it cannot be replicated quickly."
Rare earth refining produces radioactive byproducts because rare earth ores often contain thorium and uranium; managing this waste is expensive and subject to strict environmental regulation.
The U.S. has significant rare earth deposits, primarily at Mountain Pass, but most raw ore is still sent overseas for processing.

Recycling rare earths from end-of-life products — motors, electronics, magnets — is possible but currently captures less than 1% of global supply, partly because dismantling and sorting at scale remains expensive.

Heavy rare earths, including dysprosium and terbium, are less abundant than light rare earths and are primarily mined in specific regions of China; their supply is considered more strategically sensitive.

Substitution — using alternative materials that do not require rare earths — is being pursued by some manufacturers; ferrite magnets can replace neodymium magnets in some applications but are significantly weaker.
Japan, which has no domestic rare earth deposits, has invested heavily in stockpiling, recycling research, and overseas mining partnerships to reduce its dependence.
The U.S. Department of Defense considers 14 rare earth elements critical to defense applications including missile guidance, communications, and stealth technology.

Dr. Patel said the scale of the clean-energy transition — hundreds of millions of EV motors and wind turbines — will require rare earth supply to grow substantially, creating demand pressure regardless of geopolitics.

Deep-sea polymetallic nodules contain significant rare earth concentrations; deep-sea mining is being evaluated but has not yet begun at commercial scale due to environmental and technical uncertainties.

China imposed export controls on gallium and germanium, two minerals used in semiconductors, in 2023; analysts saw the move as a signal that rare earth export restrictions were a credible future policy tool.
Rare earth oxide prices are volatile; neodymium oxide prices have swung from $40 per kilogram to more than $150 per kilogram within a decade.

Dr. Patel said diversifying the refining supply chain is a 15- to 20-year project even with full government support, because the chemical engineering expertise and environmental permitting timelines are both substantial.
Australia, Canada, and several African nations have rare earth deposits that are being developed with Western government backing as alternatives to Chinese supply.
